findings.claim: The glossary tooltip on Anand Karaj reads "The Sikh wedding ceremony, meaning 'going around'".
findings.truth: Anand Karaj means 'blissful union' (anand = bliss). 'Going around' is the sense of lavan, the circling of the Guru Granth Sahib. The prose beside the tooltip and the glossary entry both give 'blissful union', so the tooltip contradicts its own lesson.
findings.evidence: internal contradiction with the same sentence and with glossary_terms[5]; spec Theme 1 Sikh perspective names the Lavan separately

findings.claim: Revision tip asks: "which two traditions use the Sigalovada Sutta as a reference?"
findings.truth: The Sigalovada Sutta is a Pali Canon text used only by Buddhism. The question has no answer.
findings.evidence: spec Theme 1 Buddhist perspective cites the Sigalovada Sutta for Buddhism alone; no other Theme 1 perspective cites it

findings.claim: The 15-mark evaluation mark scheme ends "[15 marks + SPaG 5%]".
findings.truth: 5% is the qualification-level weighting for spelling, punctuation and grammar (12 marks across the whole course). It is not a bonus added to one question. This paper carries 120 marks plus 6 for SPaG, assessed on specified extended-writing questions.
findings.evidence: spec assessment section (2.1) 'Written examination: 2 hours, 50% of qualification, 120 marks (plus 6 for spelling, punctuation and grammar)'; spec 3.1 'SPaG will be assessed in specified questions that require extended writing... 12 marks overall'

findings.claim: "examiners report that the strongest answers specifically cite Humanae Vitae" and "as many mark schemes specifically reward this".
findings.truth: Both are invented appeals to examiner reports and mark schemes. No such source is cited or citable. The underlying advice is sound and can be stated in the site's own voice; the spec does confirm that non-religious beliefs such as humanism may be applied throughout the assessment.
findings.evidence: spec 2.1 introduction on non-religious beliefs such as humanism; no examiner report exists to support the claim

findings.claim: The 15-mark evaluation mark scheme ends "[15 marks + SPaG 5%]".
findings.truth: Same error as F3. 5% is a qualification-level weighting, not marks added to this question.

findings.claim: Flashcard on Matthew 19:8-9: "Jesus acknowledged Moses permitted divorce because of hardness of hearts, but said divorce causes remarriage to be adultery."
findings.truth: Matthew 19:9 (NIV) reads: 'I tell you that anyone who divorces his wife, except for sexual immorality, and marries another woman commits adultery.' The exception clause is the whole basis of the Protestant position the lesson itself describes, so dropping it makes the card contradict the lesson body.
findings.evidence: Matthew 19:9 NIV; lesson 2 content_html 'Most Protestant churches permit divorce in cases of adultery... citing Matthew 19:8-9'

findings.claim: Triratna described as "(formally the Friends of the Western Buddhist Order)" in the tooltip and the glossary.
findings.truth: 'Formerly'. FWBO is the previous name; the order renamed itself Triratna in 2010. 'Formally' asserts that FWBO is the current formal name. Lesson 3 and the lesson 2 body text both use 'formerly'.
findings.evidence: internal inconsistency with lesson 2 body text and lesson 3 content_html

findings.claim: "In 2013, the Marriage (Same Sex Couples) Act 2013 came into force in March 2014".
findings.truth: The Act was passed in 2013 (royal assent 17 July 2013) and came into force in March 2014. The sentence gives two different commencement dates at once.
findings.evidence: Marriage (Same Sex Couples) Act 2013; first marriages 29 March 2014

findings.claim: Civil partnerships tooltip: "introduced in the UK in 2005... later extended under the Civil Partnerships Act".
findings.truth: Civil partnerships were created BY the Civil Partnership Act 2004 and became available in December 2005. There is no later 'Civil Partnerships Act' that introduced them; the 2019 extension was to opposite-sex couples. A student citing this would name a non-existent law.
findings.evidence: Civil Partnership Act 2004; first civil partnerships December 2005

findings.claim: Knowledge check stem: "The _____ is the Sikh marriage ceremony whose four stanzas describe the union of a man and woman with the divine." (answer: Lavan)
findings.truth: The Sikh marriage ceremony is the Anand Karaj, which lesson 1 teaches correctly. The Lavan is the four stanzas sung during that ceremony. The answer 'Lavan' is right for the stanzas but the stem misnames it as the ceremony. Answer index unchanged.
findings.evidence: lesson 1 content_html and glossary; lesson 3 flashcard 'The four stanzas recited at a Sikh wedding'; spec Theme 1 Sikh perspective 'The Lavan sees the married state as ideal'

findings.claim: The 15-mark evaluation mark scheme ends "[15 marks + 5 SPaG]".
findings.truth: The paper carries 6 marks for spelling, punctuation and grammar across specified extended-writing questions, not 5 marks on this question.
findings.evidence: spec assessment section 2.1 '120 marks (plus 6 for spelling, punctuation and grammar)'

findings.claim: "Examiners reward answers that show awareness of diversity within traditions".
findings.truth: An invented examiner claim. The advice itself is good and can be given in the site's own voice.
findings.evidence: no examiner report is cited or citable

findings.claim: "bhikkhuni sangha" defined in the tooltip and glossary as "Fully ordained Buddhist nun, a member of the order of nuns".
findings.truth: The bhikkhuni sangha is the order (community) of fully ordained nuns. A single nun is a bhikkhuni. The lesson's own flashcard defines it correctly as 'the order of fully ordained Buddhist nuns', and the body text uses it as a collective noun ('full reinstatement of the bhikkhuni sangha').
findings.evidence: internal contradiction with lesson 4 flashcard and body text; standard Pali usage

findings.claim: The 15-mark evaluation mark scheme ends "[15 marks + 5 SPaG]".
findings.truth: Same error as F11. The paper carries 6 SPaG marks across specified extended-writing questions.

findings.claim: "Humanist weddings (legally recognised in Scotland since 2005 and Northern Ireland since 2018... a Government consultation began in 2025)".
findings.truth: Scotland 2005 and Northern Ireland 2018 are both correct, and it is correct that England and Wales still require a separate civil ceremony. The clause 'a Government consultation began in 2025' could not be confirmed from any source available in this session. Options: (a) delete the parenthetical clause, which is not examinable content and dates the lesson; (b) leave it and verify separately.
findings.evidence: WebFetch en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Humanist_wedding confirms Scotland 2005 but carries nothing on any Government consultation

findings.claim: "the payment of a mahr (dowry) from the groom to the bride".
findings.truth: Mahr is a dower, not a dowry: a dowry travels from the bride's family to the groom, a dower from groom to bride. The lesson states the direction correctly in the same sentence, so no student is misled. Widely printed as 'dowry' in GCSE textbooks.
findings.evidence: standard usage; the sentence itself states the direction correctly

findings.claim: Galatians 3:28 quoted as "neither male nor female" in lesson 3 content, in a lesson 4 knowledge check and in a lesson 4 flashcard.
findings.truth: The NIV reads 'nor is there male and female'. 'Neither male nor female' is the KJV/ESV wording. The reference is correct everywhere and the meaning is identical, and lesson 4's main paragraph does quote the NIV wording verbatim. Not worth an edit.
findings.evidence: Galatians 3:28 NIV vs KJV/ESV; lesson 4 content_html quotes NIV correctly

findings.claim: Flashcard: "What Guru Granth Sahib reference is associated with the Sikh wedding ceremony?" answered only with GGS 773-774 (the four lavans).
findings.truth: Correct, but the spec names Guru Granth Sahib 788 as the marriage teaching for the Sikh perspective ('one light in two bodies'). GGS 788 appears nowhere in the unit, and turns up only as a distractor in a lesson 4 knowledge check. A coverage gap rather than an error.
findings.evidence: spec Theme 1 Sikh perspective: 'The nature and purpose of marriage as expressed through the Sikh marriage ceremonies and teachings: Guru Granth Sahib 788'

summary: The unit is unusually spec-faithful: every scripture reference used (Mark 10:6-8, Matthew 19:8-9, Mark 10:9, Leviticus 18:22 and 20:13, 1 Timothy 1:8-10 and 2:11-12, Galatians 3:27-29, Deuteronomy 24:1-4, Exodus 20:14, Qur'an 30:21, 17:32, 7:80-81, 2:228, 2:229, 4:1, 4:35, 40:40, Guru Granth Sahib 274, 335, 473, Rehat Maryada 11:18, Bhagavata Purana 5.5.8, Manusmriti 2.67-2.68, 5.148-155, 9.72-81, 9.192-194, Sigalovada Sutta) matches the spec's own Theme 1 citation list, and no lesson names the exam board. Dates and attributions check out (Humanae Vitae 1968 Paul VI, Lambeth 1930, CCC 1577/1935/2357-2359/2362-2363, Church of England priests 1992 vote and 1994 ordinations, women bishops permitted 2014, first British woman rabbi 1975, Quakers 2009, nine of ten Sikh Gurus married, Equality Act 2010). All 20 knowledge-check answer keys, including four match questions, are correct. The 14 fixes are one exam-fact error repeated in all four lessons (SPaG stated as a per-question bonus of 5% or 5 marks), two invented examiner or mark-scheme claims, two wrong legal statements about civil partnerships and the 2013 Act's commencement, three definition errors (Anand Karaj, bhikkhuni sangha, FWBO), one knowledge-check stem that calls the Lavan the Sikh wedding ceremony, one flashcard that drops the exception clause of Matthew 19:9, and one unanswerable revision prompt.
